title: What you still don't know
hook: open questions are part of the path

segments.voice: Yesterday: seeker, and no door required. Your line: every door stays open.

Is there a God? What happens when we die? What is the self that breathes? Which way of living is right for you? Almost a year on this path, stories, practices, seven traditions visited as a guest, weeks in the lab, and surely by now you have some answers. If you're honest, you may have fewer than when you started, and better questions. That can feel like failure, as if the point of a year like this was to arrive with everything settled. Some of the teachers you met would smile at that.
screen: `ALMOST A YEAR ON THE PATH.` → `FEWER ANSWERS, BETTER QUESTIONS.` → `THE OLD TEACHERS WOULD SMILE.`

segments.voice: Start with Socrates. In Plato's Apology, Socrates tells the jury that his friend asked the oracle at Delphi whether anyone was wiser than Socrates, and the oracle said no one was. Baffled, he went around questioning people with a reputation for wisdom. His conclusion: they thought they knew things they didn't. He, at least, didn't think he knew what he didn't know. That was his small edge. You met him on day eighty-six, saying I don't know out loud. Then, learned ignorance. In 1440 the German churchman and philosopher Nicholas of Cusa, later a cardinal, wrote a book called On Learned Ignorance, docta ignorantia. His argument, from inside his Christian faith: the infinite can't be fully grasped by a finite mind, and knowing the limits of your knowing is itself a kind of learning. Then, living the questions. The poet Rainer Maria Rilke wrote to a young poet who had sent him his questions. Be patient with what's unsolved in your heart, he advised; try to love the questions themselves; live them now, and perhaps someday you'll live your way into an answer. Why it matters here: the traditions offer answers, and people find real peace in them. This path doesn't hand you one, and it never will. It points to where the traditions keep their answers, and leaves the choosing to you. So an honest list of what you still don't know isn't a gap in the year. It's a map of where you're still alive and curious. Zhuangzi and his friend Huizi never settled whether anyone can know the joy of fish. The conversation was the point.
screen: `SOCRATES: NOT PRETENDING TO KNOW.` · `CUSA: LEARNED IGNORANCE.` · `RILKE: LOVE THE QUESTIONS.` · `A MAP OF WHERE YOU'RE CURIOUS.` · then, large: `STILL ASKING.`

segments.voice: Put the question you wrote six days ago, the one beyond the lab, at the top of a page or a note, and add two more you still can't answer, big or small: about God, death, yourself, a person in your life, how to live. Don't answer them. Read the three back slowly, and let the one that pulls hardest keep you company.
Docta ignorantia, learned ignorance: the open questions you carry, not as failure, but as a map of where you're still curious. Today's word.
Your line: still asking. Your three questions are part of the path now. That's three hundred twenty-nine.

howItsDone: Philosophers and many religious thinkers have treated honest not-knowing as part of wisdom; people on their own path often keep a short list of open questions and return to it over the years.
